_about: Scam Check rules. A weighted score from these signals decides the verdict. The on-device model only explains; it never decides. Publish new versions to https://slimboi34.github.io/scanrules-rules/scamchecker.json with a higher version number.

signals.reason: It asks you to move money to a "safe account". Banks never do this. This is always a scam.
It talks about a courier collecting your card, cash or valuables. The police and banks never do this.
phrases: put your card in an envelope

signals.reason: It asks you to install an app or let someone control your phone or computer. Never let a stranger do this.
phrases: your broadband will be cut off

signals.reason: It wants payment by gift card, crypto or a money transfer service. Real companies don't take payment this way.
It asks for a code, PIN, password or card details. Never share these with anyone, even someone who says they're from your bank.
It asks you to "confirm" or "update" your details. Scammers use this to steal them.
It tries to rush you. Scammers want you to act before you have time to think.
It tells you to keep it secret. Scammers don't want your family or your bank to warn you.
It starts like a message from your child ("Hi Mum" or "Hi Dad"). Scammers send these to thousands of people.
It says they have a new number or a broken phone. Call their old number to check it's really them.
It asks you to pay or send money quickly, often to someone else's account.
It asks for a bank transfer. Once sent, this money is very hard to get back.
It says a parcel is waiting for a small fee. Delivery firms rarely text you to pay. This is a very common scam.
It says you've won something or been chosen. If you didn't enter, you didn't win.
It offers a refund, rebate or money you are "owed". Real refunds don't need you to tap a link or give card details.
It threatens you with arrest, court, bailiffs or a fine. Scammers use fear to make you act fast.
phrases: national insurance number has been suspended

signals.reason: It promises easy or guaranteed money. Real investments never guarantee a return.
It sounds like a cold-calling trader. Never agree to work or pay on the doorstep. Get quotes from traders you choose.
They say they are the police, your bank or an official. Anyone can say that. Hang up and call back on a number you trust.
It asks you to pay a person or account you don't know. Check the name on the account first.

links._about: Hosts on these lists, or ending in .<domain>, count as official. Anything else that uses a brand's name is a look-alike.

reasons.anyLink: It has a link. Banks, delivery firms and the government rarely text you a link to pay or log in.
reasons.shortLink: The link is shortened ({{domain}}), so you can't see where it really goes.
reasons.riskyTLD: The link ends in an unusual web address ({{domain}}) that scammers use a lot.
reasons.lookalike: The web address {{domain}} looks like {{brand}}, but it isn't {{brand}}'s real website.
reasons.impersonation: It says it's from {{brand}}, but the link goes to {{domain}}, which is not {{brand}}.
reasons.brandOnCall: They said they were {{brand}}. Anyone can say that. Hang up and call {{brand}} on a number you trust.
reasons.officialLink: The link goes to {{brand}}'s real website. That's a good sign, but scammers can copy real links too.

scam.headline: This has strong signs of a scam.
scam.spoken: Scam. This has strong signs of a scam. Do not reply, do not tap any links, and do not pay.
scam.advice: Don't reply, tap links or pay. See what to do now.

likely.headline: This looks like a scam.
likely.spoken: Likely scam. This looks like a scam. Do not reply or pay until you have checked.
likely.advice: Don't reply or pay. Check by calling them back on the official number.

unsure.headline: Be careful. Some things here are worrying.
unsure.spoken: Not sure. Be careful. Some things here are worrying.
unsure.advice: If unsure, call them back on the official number. Don't use a number or link from the message.

ok.headline: We didn't find the usual scam signs.
ok.spoken: Looks OK. We didn't find the usual scam signs. If you are unsure, call them back on the official number.
ok.advice: If unsure, call them back on the official number. Find it on their real website, your bill or the back of your card.

spamText.note: Free on all big UK networks. Spells SPAM on the keypad.

phishingEmail.name: report@phishing.gov.uk
phishingEmail.note: The National Cyber Security Centre's scam email service.

reportFraud.name: Report Fraud
reportFraud.note: The UK's national fraud reporting service (it used to be called Action Fraud).
reportFraud._note: Action Fraud was replaced by Report Fraud (City of London Police) in late 2025; actionfraud.police.uk redirects. Check the phone number and URL are still current. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

bank159.note: Connects you safely to your bank's fraud team. Works for most big UK banks.

citizensAdvice.name: Citizens Advice consumer helpline
citizensAdvice._note: Check the consumer helpline number is still current.

steps.title: Don't reply, tap links or pay
steps.detail: Doing nothing is safe. A real company will still be there tomorrow.

steps.title: Hang up
steps.detail: You don't have to be polite. Then wait 5 minutes, or use a different phone, before you call anyone. Scammers can keep the line open.

steps.title: Keep the door shut
steps.detail: Ask for ID through the door or window. Don't let them in. Don't pay or agree to any work on the doorstep.

steps.title: Forward the text to 7726
steps.detail: It's free. Your phone company uses it to block the scammer.

steps.title: Forward the email to report@phishing.gov.uk
steps.detail: Then delete it. The government uses these to take scam websites down.

steps.title: Block the sender
steps.detail: In Messages: tap the name or number at the top, tap Info, then Block Caller. Then delete the message.

steps.title: Paid or shared details? Call 159 now
steps.detail: 159 puts you through to your bank's fraud team. Or call the number on the back of your card. The sooner you call, the better the chance of stopping it.

steps.title: Report it
steps.detail: Report it to Report Fraud, even if you didn't lose money. It helps stop others being caught.

steps.title: If they won't go, call the police
steps.detail: Call 101 if someone won't leave or keeps coming back. Call 999 if you feel unsafe or a crime is happening now.

steps.title: Not sure? Call them back on the official number
steps.detail: Find it on the back of your card, on a bill or on their real website. Never use a number or link from the message.

steps.title: Tell someone you trust
steps.detail: Scams happen to clever people every day. Telling family helps protect them too.

doorstep.title: Someone at the door?
doorstep.intro: Keep the door shut or on the chain. Say this:
script: Please show me your ID card through the window.
I'm not letting you in today.
I don't buy anything or agree to any work on the doorstep.
I'm going to call your company on a number I find myself.
If you don't leave, I will call the police on 101.
tips: Real workers from the water, gas or power company carry ID and won't mind waiting while you check.
Find the company's number on a bill, not on their card.
Never pay cash at the door or go to the bank with a stranger.

explain.instructions: You help older people in the UK understand possible scam messages. Plain British English a nine-year-old could follow. Short sentences. Explain only the warning signs you are given. Never say a message is safe or genuine, never change the verdict, and never tell the user to tap a link or call a number in the message.

paywall.headline: Protect the whole family
bullets: Shared with up to 5 family members through Family Sharing
Works from the Share button in Messages, Mail and Photos
Everything stays on the phone. Nothing is sent anywhere
